hook_text: Two friends walk 8 m and 5 m from the same corner. How far apart are they? Depends entirely on the corner's attitude.
clip_script: Two friends stand at the same corner of a field. One walks eight metres down one path, the other walks five down another. How far apart do they end up? You want to say Pythagoras — square, add, root. But that only works if the corner is exactly ninety degrees, and real corners never are. Here's the fix, and it's one term long. The cosine rule IS Pythagoras — eight squared plus five squared — with an attitude adjustment: minus two, times eight, times five, times cosine of the corner. Tight corner, under ninety? Cosine is positive, the correction subtracts, the friends end up CLOSER. Wide corner, past ninety? Cosine flips negative, minus times minus is plus, and they end up FURTHER apart than Pythagoras could ever say. And at exactly ninety, cosine is zero — the correction dies, and you're back to grade eight. That's also your error alarm in the exam: a wide corner must give a longer answer. If your one-hundred-and-ten-degree triangle came out shorter than the ninety-degree one, you dropped a minus sign. One formula, every triangle, no right angle required.
visual_style: Top-down animation of a dusty field: two walking figures leave glowing trails from one corner, the connecting distance stretching and shrinking as the hinge angle sweeps; the correction term flashes green when it subtracts and red when it adds.
pacing: Quick setup, beat on 'real corners never are', rhythmic tight-corner wide-corner contrast, crisp alarm-bell ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make the cosine rule the most reliable tool in your Paper Two kit.
